title: Vitamin K prophylaxis
blurb: Offer vitamin K to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding: IM as first choice, the oral regimens if parents prefer, doses from the BNFC, and consent (NICE NG235, reinstated 2026).
question: After a straightforward birth at 40 weeks, Lucy and Mark say they do not want their baby to have "an injection straight away". Their baby will be exclusively breastfed. What should the midwife explain, and what alternative can she offer?

teach.h: Preventing a rare but serious bleed
teach.body: Formally (NICE NG235 1.11.12): offer parents vitamin K prophylaxis for their babies, explaining that it prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB), a rare but serious and sometimes fatal disorder. In plain English: newborns have little vitamin K, which the blood needs to clot, so a few babies bleed unexpectedly, sometimes into the brain. One dose of vitamin K at birth (or a short oral course) prevents this. These recommendations were reintroduced to NICE guidance in 2026.

rows.label: Doses
values: Multiple doses, some after going home

teach.caption: NG235 1.11.13: give vitamin K by IM injection because this works best; if parents do not want an injection, offer oral vitamin K.

head: Baby and route
Dose
rows: 2 mg at birth, 2 mg at 4-7 days
Plus a third 2 mg dose at 1 month
1 mg at birth, then 1 mg weekly for 12 weeks
teach.caption: Oral regimens differ by product: always follow the manufacturer's instructions (NG235 1.11.13). Source: BNFC phytomenadione.
Formula-fed babies on this product need the first two doses; exclusively breastfed babies need all three.

teach.body: Any examination or treatment of the baby needs parental consent (NG235 1.11.18; Code 4.2). Explain what VKDB is, that it is rare but can be serious or fatal, that IM vitamin K works best, and what the oral option involves, including doses after discharge that must not be missed. Respect the decision. If parents decline both, record the discussion and their decision, and make sure they know the warning signs of bleeding and to seek help.

children.label: Oral course per product; plan later doses
Record, inform GP and HV, explain warning signs

items: Phytomenadione is on the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 Schedule 17 lists: registered midwives may administer it parenterally under the midwives exemption.
Midwives may also supply phytomenadione under the exemption, which supports giving oral doses.
Student midwives may administer listed exempt medicines under the direct supervision of a registered midwife.
Record the product, dose, route, time and site, and give parents a written plan for any further oral doses.

teach.body: The midwife explains VKDB and that the injection works best. Lucy and Mark still prefer to avoid it, so she offers the oral alternative. With Konakion MM Paediatric, their exclusively breastfed baby needs 2 mg at birth, 2 mg at 4 to 7 days, and 2 mg at 1 month; with NeoKay, the schedule is weekly doses for 12 weeks. She documents consent and the plan, and tells them who will give or supply the later doses so none are missed.

teach.text: The IM dose for a term baby is 1 mg; the oral Konakion dose is 2 mg per dose. And exclusively breastfed babies need the EXTRA oral dose at 1 month (Konakion) or the full 12-week weekly course (NeoKay).

items: Offer vitamin K to all babies to prevent VKDB, a rare but serious and sometimes fatal disorder.
IM injection works best: term 1 mg once at birth; preterm 400 micrograms/kg, max 1 mg.
Oral alternative: multiple doses, including after going home, per the manufacturer's instructions.
Konakion oral: 2 mg at birth and at 4-7 days, plus 2 mg at 1 month if exclusively breastfed.
Parental consent needed; record decisions; midwives can administer phytomenadione under exemption.

summary: You can now explain vitamin K deficiency bleeding and why vitamin K is offered, recommend the IM route, and set out the oral alternatives by product and feeding method. You can give the BNFC doses and handle consent and declining safely.

A.q: Why does NICE NG235 recommend giving vitamin K by intramuscular injection?
options: It is the method that works best
It is cheaper than the oral form
It avoids the need for a NIPE check
A.why: NG235 1.11.13: give vitamin K as an injection into the muscle because this is the method that works best.

whyNot.0: All treatment of the baby needs parental consent (1.11.18).
whyNot.2: Cost is not the reason NICE gives.
whyNot.3: Vitamin K has no bearing on the NIPE examination.

A.q: What is the BNFC intramuscular dose of phytomenadione for a healthy term newborn?
A.why: BNFC: neonate 1 mg by IM injection for 1 dose, given at birth.

whyNot.0: 2 mg is the oral Konakion MM Paediatric dose.
whyNot.1: 400 micrograms/kg is the preterm dose by weight, not a fixed term dose.
whyNot.2: The IM dose is a single dose at birth.

A.q: What condition does vitamin K prophylaxis prevent?
A.why: NG235 1.11.12: vitamin K prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a rare but serious and sometimes fatal disorder.

whyNot.1: Jaundice is managed under NICE CG98, not prevented by vitamin K.
whyNot.2: Hypoglycaemia is prevented by early, frequent feeding in at-risk babies.
whyNot.3: GBS is managed with intrapartum antibiotics, not vitamin K.

B.q: Baby Zara, an exclusively breastfed term baby, received 2 mg oral Konakion MM Paediatric at birth. Which further doses does she need?
options: None, as one oral dose is enough
2 mg at 4-7 days and at 1 month
A 1 mg IM dose at 1 month of age
B.why: BNFC: Konakion MM Paediatric orally: 2 mg at birth, 2 mg at 4 to 7 days, and 2 mg at 1 month for exclusively breastfed babies.

whyNot.0: Oral vitamin K needs multiple doses (NG235 1.11.13).
whyNot.1: Weekly doses for 12 weeks is the NeoKay regimen, at 1 mg per dose.
whyNot.3: The Konakion oral course continues orally, not with a later IM dose.

B.q: Baby Leo was born at 32 weeks weighing 1.6 kg. What is the BNFC intramuscular vitamin K dose?
options: A fixed 1 mg dose at birth
B.why: BNFC: preterm neonate 400 micrograms/kg IM for 1 dose (maximum 1 mg) at birth. For Leo that is 640 micrograms.

whyNot.1: Preterm babies are dosed by weight, not a fixed 1 mg.
whyNot.2: Oral dosing is for healthy babies whose parents decline IM; this asks for the IM dose.
whyNot.3: This is not the BNFC preterm dose.

B.q: Parents of Baby Ari accept oral vitamin K. Ari spits out most of the NeoKay capsule contents 20 minutes after the dose. What should the midwife do?
options: Record a full dose as given
Give an IM dose instead without asking
Wait for the next weekly dose
B.why: BNFC: if the baby spits out the dose or is sick within 3 hours of oral administration, a replacement dose should be given.

whyNot.0: Recording a full dose would be inaccurate; protection may be inadequate.
whyNot.1: Changing to IM needs fresh parental consent.
whyNot.2: Waiting a week leaves the baby unprotected.

C.q: Ella and Tom decline both IM and oral vitamin K after a full discussion. Their baby is well. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give the injection quietly during the NIPE check
Record their decision; explain warning signs
Refer to safeguarding for refusing treatment
Delay discharge home until they agree to it
C.why: Treatment needs parental consent (NG235 1.11.18). After an informed discussion, respect and document the decision, inform the GP and health visitor, and make sure parents know when to seek help.

whyNot.0: Giving it without consent would be unlawful and a breach of the Code.
whyNot.2: An informed decision to decline vitamin K is not by itself a safeguarding concern.
whyNot.3: Withholding discharge to pressure parents is coercive and not justified.

C.q: A student midwife asks whether a midwife needs a prescription to give IM vitamin K to a newborn. What is the best answer?
options: Yes, a doctor must prescribe each dose given
No, but a signed PGD is needed first
No, it is on the midwives exemption list
Yes, unless the baby was born at home
C.why: Human Medicines Regulations 2012 Schedule 17: registered midwives may administer parenteral phytomenadione in the course of their professional practice under the midwives exemption.

whyNot.0: Phytomenadione is on the Schedule 17 midwives exemption list.
whyNot.1: A PGD is not needed for a medicine covered by the midwives exemption.
whyNot.3: The exemption does not depend on place of birth.

C.q: Priya chooses oral NeoKay for her exclusively breastfed baby. Which schedule should the midwife explain?
options: 1 mg at birth, then 1 mg weekly for 12 weeks
A single 1 mg dose at birth for a breastfed baby
2 mg at birth and at 4-7 days
1 mg at birth and 1 mg at 6 weeks
C.why: BNFC: NeoKay for exclusively breastfed babies: 1 mg at birth, then 1 mg every week for 12 weeks.

whyNot.1: A single NeoKay dose at birth covers the first week for babies not exclusively breastfed; breastfed babies need weekly doses.
whyNot.2: 2 mg at birth and at 4-7 days is the Konakion MM Paediatric regimen.
whyNot.3: This schedule is not in the BNFC.

reteach.title: One jab or several drops
reteach.question: Vitamin K comes down to one choice for parents: one injection, or several oral doses. What does each involve?

blocks.body: ONE JAB: 1 mg IM at birth for a term baby, the method that works best, and nothing more to remember. SEVERAL DROPS: oral doses at birth and later, some at home; the number depends on the product and whether the baby is exclusively breastfed. Whichever they choose, it needs their consent and a clear record.

blocks.h: Oral plan for an exclusively breastfed baby (Konakion)

blocks.text: "Oral is the same as IM" is wrong: NICE says IM works best, and oral protection depends on every dose being given.

explain.body: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding is rare but serious and sometimes fatal. Offer prophylaxis to parents for all babies and explain its purpose.

test.q: Which description of vitamin K deficiency bleeding matches NICE NG235?
test.why: NG235 1.11.12: VKDB is a rare but serious and sometimes fatal disorder.

whyNot.0: VKDB is rare, and can be serious.
whyNot.2: VKDB can be serious or fatal.

explain.body: Term: 1 mg IM once at birth. Preterm: 400 micrograms/kg IM (maximum 1 mg) at birth; IV may be used in very low birth weight preterm babies if IM is not possible, followed by oral doses.

test.q: A preterm baby weighs 2 kg. What is the IM vitamin K dose according to the BNFC?
test.why: 400 micrograms/kg x 2 kg = 800 micrograms, which is below the 1 mg maximum.

whyNot.0: 400 micrograms is the dose for a 1 kg baby.
whyNot.1: 1 mg is the maximum and the term dose; this baby's weight-based dose is lower.
whyNot.3: 2 mg is the oral Konakion dose and exceeds the IM maximum.

explain.body: Konakion MM Paediatric: 2 mg at birth, 2 mg at 4-7 days, plus 2 mg at 1 month if exclusively breastfed. NeoKay: 1 mg at birth; if exclusively breastfed, 1 mg weekly for 12 weeks. Replace a dose spat out or vomited within 3 hours.

test.q: Within what time of an oral vitamin K dose should a replacement dose be given if the baby vomits?
test.why: BNFC: if the baby spits out the dose or is sick within three hours of administration, a replacement dose should be given.

whyNot.0: 30 minutes is shorter than the BNFC window.
whyNot.1: 1 hour is shorter than the BNFC window.
whyNot.3: 24 hours is longer than the BNFC window.

explain.body: Parental consent is needed for any examination or treatment of the baby. Midwives may administer parenteral phytomenadione and supply it under the Schedule 17 midwives exemptions. Record decisions, including declining.

test.q: Before a midwife gives IM vitamin K, what must she obtain?
test.why: NG235 1.11.18: any examination or treatment of the baby should be undertaken with the parents' consent. Phytomenadione is covered by the midwives exemption, so no prescription is needed.

whyNot.1: Phytomenadione is on the midwives exemption list.
whyNot.2: A second signature is not a requirement for this exemption.
whyNot.3: Clotting tests are not needed before prophylaxis.
